newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian crime down but woes remain, official says.
newsitem.headline: Russian crime down but woes remain, official says.

text.p: The wave of crime gripping Russia in recent years has eased in 1997 but lack of state control in the Far East has led to huge losses in potential customs duties, Russia's interior minister said on Tuesday.

During the first four months of the year the number of registered crimes in Russia fell by 10 percent to 795,000 cases, with murders down six percent over the same period a year ago, Anatoly Kulikov told a news conference.
"This positive tendency was first seen in 1995 and 1996. The first quarter confirms that this is really a trend," Kulikov said.

The trend has yet to register with the Russian public however. Russia has experienced an upsurge in crime since the fall of the Soviet Union and many Russians say they now fear for their safety as never before.
Kulikov said that violent battles between rival gangs had risen this year, as had home robberies and kidnapping.
But he said police had made important progress in solving several high-profile murders arranged by organised criminal groups while investigations continued into other past crimes.
"We haven't closed a single (unsolved) case of these murders from 1995-96," he said.

But Kulikov said he detected a major problem in law enforcement efforts in the Russian Far East region, located a week's rail journey from Moscow and which is ever more oriented toward Asia rather than European Russia.

"There is a very serious danger of the Far East breaking away, including from the influence of the federal centre on the collection of customs duties," said Kulikov, who visited the region earlier this month.

He said there was a "blatant squandering of fish and seafood" because of a lack of control over Russian territorial waters. He said this failing led to an estimated two billion dollars of goods being traded outside Russian customs' control.
Such trade might involve a Russian firm fishing in the region and exporting directly outside of official channels at below-market prices.
The solution to the problem, he said, was appointing a federal official to coordinate the work of tax police, customs, and other government offices.

During his travels, Kulikov said he also visited one local police department in the remote Chukotka Peninsula facing Alaska where officers are paid with a delay of six months. Federal police officers usually get paid one or two months late.
